answer: Designing thin-walled aluminum parts for CNC demands control of geometry (tool-access radii and wall slenderness), anticipation of workpiece/machine compliance that drives chatter and rubbing, and management of heat, burrs, and residual stress. Use generous internal fillets to allow stiff, short tools; account for thermal expansion in tight fits; plan for residual-stress release when removing a lot of stock; and expect burrs to stop tight assemblies unless you call out deburring. Where evidence exists, the sections below translate forum-proven pitfalls into CAD-stage decisions and physics rationales.

Decision rule-of-thumb: use climb milling when the machine axes are backlash-free and the whole cut system (machine, tool, workholding, and workpiece) is sufficiently rigid; prefer conventional milling when there is any meaningful backlash, flexible fixturing/gantry, or when you need to avoid pull-in and path overtravel. For chatter and tool deflection, prioritize rigidity and avoid too-light finishing passes that only rub. For manual mills with backlash, plan conventional milling or one-direction approaches. For burr-sensitive fits and cosmetic faces, plan deburring and realistic finish callouts regardless of direction. Chip-thickness/heat: very thin chips (from light cuts or poor engagement) increase rubbing and heat, accelerating wear; direction choice matters less than maintaining a real chip load. Abrasive materials (e.g., FR‑4, mill scale analogs) accelerate wear; pick materials and allowances accordingly.

Deep pockets and tall, narrow ribs are limited by rotating-tool geometry (inside corner radii), by stiffness/dynamics (tool and wall deflection leading to chatter), and by evacuation/thermal needs (chip removal and coolant access). Avoid specifying sharp internal corners, control minimum feature thickness to prevent “slivers,” and design paths for chips and coolant to reach and exit deep cavities. When function allows, prefer simpler lightening geometries (through-holes/patterns) over tall thin ribs. The evidence below supports corner-radius constraints, dynamics risks from too-light/heavy cuts, and chip/coolant access needs; gaps remain on numeric L/D and rib aspect-ratio limits and material-specific rib guidance.

For small-batch parts, adding chamfers and edge breaks primarily increases fixed, front-loaded costs (programming, setup, tool sourcing) that are weakly amortized over few pieces; it can also add runtime for extra tool changes, manual deburring where burrs matter, and inspection if many explicit chamfer callouts are specified. Light, tiny chamfers raise the risk of rubbing/heat that shortens tool life and may force slower, chatter-averse passes on thin edges, further increasing cycle time. Effects are most pronounced at low quantities and in abrasive materials; evidence on inspection-time impact and thin-wall chamfer chatter is limited in the sources.

For robust traceability between design and machining, define a dedicated, datum-referenced marking pad on each part, and tie all marks (text, 2D codes, or IDs) to the same A/B/C datums used in machining. Use jigs/fixtures to ensure repeatable location of the mark and the part; avoid using bolt patterns as locators and prefer pin-and-slot concepts for poka-yoke. Expect coolant exposure on metal jobs and specify corrosion controls (e.g., post-marking passivation on susceptible alloys). Avoid raster-printed labels for fine codes; use direct part marking methods that preserve edge fidelity. Note: evidence supports datum alignment, fixture repeatability, coolant/corrosion risks, and assembly/locating practices; there are knowledge gaps on fatigue from dot peen/laser, Data Matrix readability on oily surfaces, and RFID near metal/coolant.

Example failure: A turned motor shaft uses two radial ball bearings on 20 mm journals, a ground spacer, and a locknut against a shoulder. The seat diameters drifted a few microns undersize across a batch due to a systematic setup bias and gradual tool wear, while the journals had a rougher-than-intended finish. At assembly in a cool shop, the bearings were warmed and slipped on, but once temperatures equalized the interference was higher than planned, creating high press loads and brinelling risk; on other units, a small worst-case clearance at one seat allowed micro-fretting. The spacer and shoulder stack left the inner races slightly over-preloaded. In service, temperature changes further altered the fit tightness. The result was noisy bearings and premature wear even though individual drawing tolerances looked acceptable.

No single minimum inside bend radius can be stated for 16‑gauge stainless in air bending without the alloy/temper and its ductility data. Evidence indicates the minimum radius must be derived from the material’s tensile reduction‑of‑area (ductility) per standard bend‑limit formulas, and cracking risk rises sharply at stress concentrations near the bend. There is no evidence here tying V‑die opening, punch tip radius, springback magnitude, tonnage, or grain‑direction effects to quantified values for 16‑gauge stainless, so those remain knowledge gaps.

Evidence specific to FDM/PLA overhangs is sparse in the provided frames; most insights are general mechanics and materials principles that map to overhang support decisions. The key takeaways are: design to limit deflection (sag) rather than only preventing failure, distribute supports under broad spans, expect reduced strength/adhesion in FDM parts when planning support contact and removal, and balance adhesion versus removability at support interfaces. Quantitative PLA rules (e.g., >45° limits, layer height vs nozzle diameter, bridging spans, fan CFM) are not covered and remain knowledge gaps.
